# Spherical Harmonics Optimization

Also called: SH Optimization, View-Dependent Color Optimization

## Overview
Spherical Harmonics (SH) Optimization encompasses methods that adjust, compress, or replace the SH coefficients used to represent view-dependent color in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [G]. It solves the problems of high memory consumption, training instability with sparse views, and limited expressiveness of fixed-basis SH functions. It differs from [Color and Appearance Modeling](14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md) by focusing specifically on the optimization dynamics, storage efficiency, and analytical derivation of the SH parameters rather than just their definition.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family inherit the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting representation and rendering pipeline from [Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints](15421-scene-representation-and-geometry-constraints.md) [G]. The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of $\mathbf{c}_i(\omega)$ and potentially $\alpha_i$, moving beyond the fixed SH coefficients used in base 3DGS [G]. Common strategies include post-processing transformation [DAVIGS](12021-davigs.md), factorized illumination [3iGS](13977-3igs-factorised-tensorial-illumination-for-3d-gaussian-splat.md), image-conditioned modulation [SWAG](14315-swag-splatting-in-the-wild-images-with-appearance-conditione.md), and neural field substitution [Compact View-dependent Color](12904-compact-view-dependent-color.md) [G].

## Subtopics

### [First-order Spherical Harmonics Distillation](9467-first-order-spherical-harmonics-distillation.md)
First-order Spherical Harmonics (SH) Distillation is a compression technique that reduces the directional appearance complexity of 3D Gaussian primitives by distilling high-order SH coefficients (typically degree 3) into a lower-order representation (typically degree 1). It solves the problem of excessive storage and computational overhead associated with third-order SH in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by training a "student" model with first-order SH to approximate the radiance output of a pretrained "teacher" model with third-order SH. Unlike [Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization](14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md), which reduces precision via codebooks, or [Adaptive SH Regularization](16786-adaptive-sh-regularization.md), which prunes coefficients based on importance, distillation preserves the full first-order basis while transferring knowledge from the higher-order domain.

### [Explicit Camera Jacobian Derivation](10077-explicit-camera-jacobian-derivation.md)
This method derives analytical Jacobians of the SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussian primitives to enable efficient gradient-based camera pose optimization in SLAM systems. It sets itself apart from prior ray-intersection methods by providing the first analytical Jacobian for EWA splatting and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), ensuring minimal parameterization via Lie algebra and avoiding the overhead of automatic differentiation.

### [Efficient Multi-View Training for 3D Gaussian Splatting](13982-efficient-multi-view-training-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md)
This method enables stable optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by processing multiple training images per iteration, addressing the high variance of gradients inherent in the standard single-view approach. Unlike standard 3DGS which renders one image per iteration due to rasterization overhead, this method uses thread-efficient partial rendering to gather pixels from multiple views without idle thread waste, while replacing the standard Adaptive Density Control (ADC) with a 3D-space compatible densification strategy to prevent arithmetic errors between different image planes.

### [Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization](14181-spherical-harmonics-vector-quantization.md)
Spherical Harmonics Vector Quantization (SH VQ) is a compression technique for 3D Gaussian Splatting that replaces per-splat SH coefficients with indices pointing to a shared palette of distinct SH vectors, significantly reducing memory footprint at the cost of minor lighting artifacts. Unlike methods that exploit spatial correlation between neighbors, SH VQ treats each Gaussian's SH-AC vector independently, mapping it to the nearest codevector in a pre-computed palette. This approach is distinct from [Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation](16750-closed-form-scene-appearance-estimation.md) which estimates appearance analytically, and [Adaptive SH Regularization](16786-adaptive-sh-regularization.md) which constrains coefficient magnitudes during training; instead, SH VQ operates as a post-processing or offline optimization step to reduce storage and transmission size.

### [Closed-Form Scene Appearance Estimation](16750-closed-form-scene-appearance-estimation.md)
This method solves for the spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients of mesh vertices by formulating a global weighted least-squares problem that jointly fits RGB observations from all calibrated training views. It distinguishes itself from iterative gradient-based optimization by providing an analytical solution to the appearance estimation sub-problem, utilizing adaptive regularization to handle varying angular support across the mesh surface.

### [Adaptive SH Regularization](16786-adaptive-sh-regularization.md)
Adaptive SH Regularization is a technique used during the optimization of Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients in 3D Gaussian Splatting to prevent overfitting when training views are sparse or unevenly distributed. It selectively suppresses higher-order SH components ($l > 0$) for primitives lacking sufficient directional support from camera viewpoints, while preserving the zeroth-order (DC) component. Unlike methods that rely solely on iterative optimization with fixed SH complexity, this approach explicitly adapts the regularization strength based on the geometric relationship between the primitive and the available viewing directions.

### [Geometry-Guided Appearance Modeling](20876-geometry-guided-appearance-modeling.md)
Geometry-Guided Appearance Modeling (GAM) is a method for predicting view-dependent colors in 3D Gaussian Splatting by conditioning the appearance on explicit geometric cues, such as surface normals and learned geometric features derived from a Signed Distance Field (SDF). It solves the limitation of standard Spherical Harmonics (SH), which often fail to capture fine-grained geometric details and high-frequency reflections. Unlike its sibling [Spherical Harmonics Optimization](14206-spherical-harmonics-optimization.md), which relies on fixed basis functions, GAM replaces or augments SH with a geometry-conditioned Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP).

#### SH Degree Zero Optimization
**Definition:** Setting the maximum degree of Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients to 0 to remove superfluous operations and improve training speed, as higher-degree SH coefficients for color remain unchanged during training [S1, unofficial].
**Step:** Modify the model code to delete operations relative to the max degree in the model and set the max degree parameter to 0 [S1, unofficial].
**Pitfall:** In the original 3D Gaussian Splatting model, features represented by SH coefficients with degree > 0 are unchanged during all training, making them useless [S1, unofficial].
**Number:** Directly changing the max degree to 0 yields a 16.25% improvement compared to the default. With specific changing code, it yields a 16.57% improvement but increases CPU-GPU process time [S1, unofficial].

## Background
The use of Spherical Harmonics for view-dependent shading in computer graphics dates back to the 1990s, with foundational work by Ramamoorthi and Hanrahan on efficient representation of view-dependent effects [G]. In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023, SH coefficients are used to encode per-Gaussian color variation [G]. Subsequent research has focused on optimizing these coefficients for speed, memory, and robustness, leading to the methods described above.
